claim: Human papillomaviruses are DNA viruses that are linked to 5% of human cancers.
source: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are DNA viruses which are linked to 5% of human cancers (McBride, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McBride, 2017

claim: Mucosotropic high-risk HPVs have been associated with cervical cancer, other anogenital cancers, and a subset of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
source: Mucosotropic high-risk HPVs, a group which includes HPV16 and HPV18, have been associated with malignancies, mainly cervical cancer, other anogenital cancers, and a subset of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (zur Hausen, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to zur Hausen, 2009

claim: Papillomaviruses abundantly colonize human epithelia without causing apparent pathology.
source: In addition to representing a significant source of pathogenesis, it is clear that papillomaviruses also abundantly colonize human epithelia without causing an apparent pathology (Hannigan et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hannigan et al., 2015

claim: Differentiation of stratified epithelia is essential for the productive HPV replication cycle.
source: Since differentiation of stratified epithelia is essential for the productive HPV replication cycle (Roden and Stern, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roden and Stern, 2018

claim: The outcome of HPV infection is greatly influenced by the host immune system and inflammation induced by tissue damage.
source: Furthermore, the outcome of HPV infection is greatly influenced by the host immune system and inflammation induced by tissue damage that is required in order to expose the underlying basal layer to the virus (Amador-Molina et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amador-Molina et al., 2013

claim: A mouse specific papillomavirus (MmuPV1) was discovered.
source: This is now possible due to the discovery of a mouse specific papillomavirus (MmuPV1) (Ingle et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ingle et al., 2011 and Hu et al., 2017

claim: The mouse papillomavirus genome is similar to human papillomavirus genome, with the exception of the lack of E5 gene in the mouse virus.
source: Even though the genome of the human and mouse papillomavirus is similar, with the exception of the lack of E5 gene in the mouse virus, HPVs, and MmuPV1 do indeed show differences at the level of nucleotide sequences (Joh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joh et al., 2011

claim: HPVs and MmuPV1 show differences at the level of nucleotide sequences.
source: Even though the genome of the human and mouse papillomavirus is similar, with the exception of the lack of E5 gene in the mouse virus, HPVs, and MmuPV1 do indeed show differences at the level of nucleotide sequences (Joh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joh et al., 2011

claim: Subclinical MmuPV1 infections have been previously reported.
source: Additionally, subclinical MmuPV1 infections have also been previously reported (Hu et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2017 and Xue et al., 2017

claim: Cre recombinase facilitates YFP expression in MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox transfected MEFs.
source: As expected, we detected the function of the Cre recombinase which facilitates the YFP expression in the MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox transfected cells by immunofluorescence (IF) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid undergoes recombination after Cre expression.
source: Additionally, we isolated DNA from these transfected cells and determined the PCR amplification of the Cre sequence and sequence flanking the Cre cassette (Cre loss), showing the recombination of the MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid after Cre expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MmuPV1 viral transcripts E1/E4, L1 and E6 are present in MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox transfected MEFs but not in pBABE-GFP transfected cells.
source: Lastly, we detected the presence of MmuPV1 viral transcripts E1/E4, L1 and E6 via RT-PCR analysis in MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox transfected cells but not in pBABE-GFP transfected cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figures 1C and 1D

claim: The constructed MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid can lead to reporter activation, Cre-excision, and MmuPV1 genome recircularization in vitro.
source: Together, these results validate that the constructed MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid can indeed lead to reporter activation, Cre-excision, and MmuPV1 genome recircularization in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by the in vitro experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Infection with MmuPV1 is mainly cleared by the functions of the CD8+T cell-dependent adaptive immunity.
source: It is known that infection with MmuPV1 is mainly cleared by the functions of the CD8+T cell-dependent adaptive immunity (Handisurya et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Handisurya et al., 2014

claim: Immunocompromised mice are more susceptible to the mouse papillomavirus.
source: Therefore, immunocompromised mice are more susceptible to the mouse papillomavirus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statement about CD8+T cell-dependent immunity clearing MmuPV1 infection

claim: UV-B radiation suppresses the adaptive immune response, whereas the innate immune response remains largely unaffected.
source: UV-B was shown to suppress the adaptive immune response, whereas the innate immune response remains largely unaffected (Uberoi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uberoi et al., 2016

claim: Characteristic clones of YFP-expressing cell populations were observed in the skin indicative of heritable YFP activation in a skin basal cell.
source: We observed characteristic clones of YFP-expressing cell population in the skin indicative of heritable YFP activation in a skin basal cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Clones of YFP-expressing cells were most prominent at day 3 and day 5 after plasmid delivery.
source: Clones were most prominent at day 3 and day 5 after plasmid delivery (Figure 2B, indicated with white lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B

claim: YFP+ cells can be followed at later time points after plasmid delivery.
source: Additionally, we were able to follow-up YFP+ cells at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by the longitudinal observations described in the text

claim: The model can be used as an in vivo lineage-tracing model for MmuPV1, where virus-hosting cells and their progeny can be individually observed via their genetically induced YFP expression.
source: These results indicate that our model can indeed be used as an in vivo lineage-tracing model for MmuPV1, where virus-hosting cells and their progeny can be individually observed via their genetically induced YFP expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing YFP expression in cells over time

claim: E6/E7 transcripts started to appear as early as 3 days post-delivery and peaked around day 7 post-delivery in cells that have taken up the MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid.
source: We observed that in the cells that have taken up the MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid, E6/E7 transcripts started to appear as early as 3 days post-delivery (p.d.) and peaked around day 7 p.d. (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3A

claim: E1/E4 transcripts were detected at day 5 post-delivery onward and peaked at day 10 post-delivery in cells that have taken up the MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid.
source: whereas the E1/E4 transcripts were detected at day 5 p.d. onward and peaked at day 10 p.d. (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3B

claim: No MmuPV1 viral transcripts were detected in cells that have taken up the CAG-Cre plasmid.
source: Furthermore, we did not detect any of the tested MmuPV1 viral transcripts in the cells that have taken up the CAG-Cre plasmid since the viral genome of MmuPV1 is lacking in this control plasmid (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: The majority of the observed signal for MmuPV1-E6/7 and E1/E4 was viral RNA signal rather than viral genomic DNA signal.
source: Additionally, we distinguished the viral RNA signal from the viral genomic DNA signal by treating the tissue sections with DNAse and/or RNAse prior to probe hybridization in which we confirmed that the majority of the observed signal for MmuPV1-E6/7 and E1/E4 was indeed viral RNA signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data with DNAse/RNAse treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: The Cre loss and the MmuPV1-L1 sequences were detected at day 5 and day 10 samples of the skin surface.
source: However, we detected the Cre loss and the MmuPV1-L1 sequences at day 5 and day 10 samples of the skin surface (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3E

claim: CAG-Cre control samples showed no signal for Cre loss or MmuPV1-L1 sequences.
source: whereas CAG-Cre control samples showed no signal as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: The amount of correctly recombined MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid after Cre expression is rather low but still present in vivo.
source: However, since the level of the detected signal is considerably low, as can be seen in Figure 3E or Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, we believe that the amount of correctly recombined MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid after Cre expression is rather low but still present in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the low signal levels observed in PCR data

claim: At day 30 time point, no viral genome was detected on swabs of the tail skin even though YFP+ cells were still detected at this time point.
source: At day 30 time point, we did not detect any viral genome on swabs of the tail skin even though we still detect YFP+ cells at this time point, albeit at low levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR and flow cytometry data

claim: The absence of viral genome detection at day 30 might be indicative of the greatly reduced presence (below limit of detection) or clearance of the virus on the skin.
source: This might be indicative of the greatly reduced presence (below limit of detection) or clearance of the virus on the skin.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the absence of viral genome detection at day 30

claim: Virion-like structures were visualized in the perinuclear area of epithelial cells in all the MmuPV1-Cre treated mice.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we were able to visualize virion-like structures in the perinuclear area of epithelial cells in all the MmuPV1-Cre treated mice, whereas none of these structures were observed in mice treated with the control CAG-Cre plasmid (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3F

claim: No virion-like structures were observed in mice treated with the control CAG-Cre plasmid.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we were able to visualize virion-like structures in the perinuclear area of epithelial cells in all the MmuPV1-Cre treated mice, whereas none of these structures were observed in mice treated with the control CAG-Cre plasmid (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Both numbers and percentages of YFP+ cells were much higher in MmuPV1 samples at day 5 post-delivery, which decreased overtime as seen at day 10 and day 30 post-delivery.
source: We found that both numbers and percentages of YFP+ cells were much higher in MmuPV1 samples at day 5 p.d., which decreased overtime as seen at day 10 and day 30 p.d.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: pCAG-Cre samples only start to have increased YFP+ cells around day 10 post-delivery.
source: Whereas, pCAG-Cre samples only start to have increased YFP+ cells around day 10 p.d. (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: MmuPV1-harboring cells exhibit significantly increased levels of Ki-67 around day 5 post-delivery compared to other time points.
source: Furthermore, coinciding with the increased number of YFP+ cells, we observed that MmuPV1-harboring cells exhibit significantly increased levels of Ki-67 around day 5 p.d. compare to other time points (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cells harboring MmuPV1-Cre plasmid exhibit higher proliferation around day 5 post-delivery compared to the cells harboring CAG-Cre control plasmid.
source: We further directly visualized Ki-67-positive cells by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in the regions of infected skin where we previously detected the MmuPV1 transcripts via RNAscope and observed that the cells harboring MmuPV1-Cre plasmid indeed exhibit higher proliferation around day 5 p.d. compare to the cells harboring CAG-Cre control plasmid (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Papillomaviruses have previously been reported to reduce MHC-I expression in vitro.
source: Papillomaviruses have previously been reported to reduce MHC-I expression, but evidence was generated in vitro (Georgopoulos et al., 2000; Heller et al., 2011; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Georgopoulos et al., 2000; Heller et al., 2011; Li et al., 2010

claim: YFP+ cells of MmuPV1-treated tissues exhibit significantly lower expression of MHC-I molecules at day 5 post-delivery.
source: Interestingly, we observed significantly lower expression of MHC-I molecules on the YFP+ cells of MmuPV1-treated tissues at day 5 p.d., whereas YFP+ cells in control treated tissues exhibit increased MHC-I expression at this time point, presumable due to YFP neo-antigen expression (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: YFP+ cells in control treated tissues exhibit increased MHC-I expression at day 5 post-delivery, presumably due to YFP neo-antigen expression.
source: Interestingly, we observed significantly lower expression of MHC-I molecules on the YFP+ cells of MmuPV1-treated tissues at day 5 p.d., whereas YFP+ cells in control treated tissues exhibit increased MHC-I expression at this time point, presumable due to YFP neo-antigen expression (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data and speculation about YFP neo-antigen

claim: The effects of MmuPV1 on proliferation and MHC-I expression waned at later time points.
source: These effects waned at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by the flow cytometry data showing changes over time

claim: MmuPV1 results agree with previous in vitro studies and indicate a possible immune evasion strategy by the MmuPV1 where the virus is causing a decreased expression of MHC-I molecules on the cell surface to reduce the antigen exposure to the immune cells.
source: Our results agree with previous in vitro studies and indicate a possible immune evasion strategy by the MmuPV1 where the virus is causing a decreased expression of MHC-I molecules on the cell surface to reduce the antigen exposure to the immune cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the MHC-I expression data and comparison with previous studies

claim: The differences in proliferation and MHC-I expression were specific to the YFP+ cells within the tissue.
source: It is important to note, that the differences in proliferation and MHC- I expression were specific to the YFP + cells within the tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparison of YFP+ and YFP- cells within the same tissues

claim: No significant difference in Ki-67 and MHC-I levels was observed between time points or between the YFP- cell population of the MmuPV1 plasmid-treated tissue and the CAG-Cre plasmid-treated tissue.
source: We observed no significant difference between time points or between the YFP- cell population of the MmuPV1 plasmid-treated tissue and the CAG-Cre plasmid-treated tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: Any differences observed in proliferation and MHC-I expression are specific to plasmid uptake.
source: These results suggest that any differences observed are specific to plasmid uptake.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of YFP+ and YFP- cells

claim: During early acute infection, MmuPV1 causes increased proliferation which may be accompanied by decreased antigen presentation.
source: Together, these results indicate that during early acute infection, MmuPV1 causes increased proliferation which may be accompanied by decreased antigen presentation.
evidence: The claim is based on the Ki-67 and MHC-I expression data

claim: The novel in vivo lineage-tracing model can be used as a tool to answer key questions in the field of MmuPV1 biology.
source: Additionally, here we show that our novel in vivo lineage-tracing model can be used as a tool to answer such key questions in the field of MmuPV1 biology.
evidence: The claim is supported by the proof-of-concept experiments demonstrating the utility of the model

claim: The ability to trace MmuPV-1 harboring cells and their progeny by microscopy, as well as to quantify and analyze by means of flow-cytometry renders this model a suitable and convenient tool for answering a variety of outstanding questions in papillomavirus biology.
source: We propose that the ability to trace MmuPV-1 harboring cells and their progeny by microscopy, as well as to quantify and analyze by means of flow-cytometry renders this model a suitable and convenient tool for answering a variety of outstanding questions in papillomavirus biology (Lambert et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on the demonstrated capabilities of the model and supported by a citation to Lambert et al., 2020

claim: The novel model can be used to investigate the early effects of papillomavirus on the target cells, transcriptional and phenotypic changes of the papillomavirus-harboring cells during the acute phase of the infection, and investigate the initial viral-host immune interactions.
source: Particularly, we believe that the novel model described here can be used to investigate the early effects of papillomavirus on the target cells, transcriptional and phenotypic changes of the papillomavirus-harboring cells during the acute phase of the infection, and investigate the initial viral-host immune interactions.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future applications of the model

claim: R26R-lox-STOP-lox-eYFP mice were of a pure C57BL/6 genetic background.
source: R26R-lox-STOP-lox-eYFP (Jackson lab stock number #006148, https://www.jax.org/strain/006148) immunocompetent mice, obtained from the mouse facility of the Cyprus Institute of Neurology and Genetics (CING), were of a pure C57BL/6 genetic background.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the mouse strain used

claim: All mice were used at 6–12 weeks of age and were sex- and age-matched within experiments.
source: All mice were used at 6–12 weeks of age and were sex- and age-matched within experiments.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design

claim: A single dose of 1000 mJ/cm2 UV-B irradiation was applied for immunosuppression.
source: The back skin of 6–9 weeks old female R26R-lox-STOP-lox-eYFP mice were shaved and a single dose of 1000 mJ/cm2 UV-B irradiation was applied for immunosuppression as previously described (Dorfer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental protocol and is supported by a citation to Dorfer et al., 2021

claim: 2 × 10^9 DNA copies of MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox or CAG-Cre plasmid in a 10 µl of PBS solution were applied at the base of the tail skin by a superficial scarification with a pipette tip.
source: Following the UV-B radiation, the mice were given at the same day with 2 × 109 DNA copies of MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox or CAG-Cre plasmid in a 10 µl of PBS solution applied at the base of the tail skin by a superficial scarification with a pipette tip to expose the tail basal layer.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental protocol

claim: Tail skin was selected for plasmid delivery for practical reasons (ability to track area where plasmid was delivered and fewer hairs which place barriers on cell dissociation for FACS experiments).
source: Tail skin was selected for plasmid delivery for practical reasons (ability to track area where plasmid was delivered and fewer hairs which place barriers on cell dissociation for FACS experiments).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement explaining the rationale for experimental design

claim: Frozen tissues were sectioned at 17 microns thick using a cryostat.
source: Frozen tissues were then sectioned (17 microns thick) using a cryostat and mounted on the positively charged Thermo Scientific SuperFrost Plus Adhesive slides.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental protocol

claim: MmuPV1 viral transcripts were detected using RNAscope 2.5 HD Assay-Brown with probes specific for MmuPV1 E6/E7 and for MmuPV1 E1/E4.
source: MmuPV1 viral transcripts were detected using RNAscope 2.5 HD Assay-Brown (cat. no. 322300) (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Newark, CA) according to manufacturer instructions with probes specific for MmuPV1 E6/E7 (Cat #409771) and for MmuPV1 E1/E4 (Cat #473281) as described previously (Spurgeon and Lambert, 2019; Xue et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental protocol and is supported by citations to Spurgeon and Lambert, 2019 and Xue et al., 2017

claim: Nonparametric 2-way ANOVA test was performed and statistical significance was considered at p<0.05.
source: Nonparametric 2-way ANOVA test was performed and statistical significance was considered at p<0.05.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the statistical analysis method

claim: All the experiments were performed using at least three biological replicates.
source: All the experiments were performed using at least three biological replicates.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design

claim: The MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid was delivered to the tail skin of reporter R26R-lox-STOP-lox-eYFP mice.
source: We have created an MmuPV1-lox-Cre-lox plasmid which we deliver to the tail skin of reporter R26R-lox-STOP-lox-eYFP mice.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental approach

claim: Expression of self-deleting Cre from the plasmid results in recombination of the loxP sites and excision of the sequence flanked by the loxP sites.
source: Expression of self-deleting Cre from the plasmid results in recombination of the loxP sites and excision of the sequence flanked by the loxP sites.

claim: Introduction of the plasmid in mouse cells leads to the production of Cre recombinase and loss of the Cre sequence and its promoter from the plasmid and recircularization of the MmuPV1 genome, and the loss of the stop codon upstream of the yellow florescence protein (YFP) gene.
source: Therefore, introduction of the plasmid in mouse cells leads to the production of Cre recombinase and loss of the Cre sequence and its promoter from the plasmid and, more importantly, recircularization of the MmuPV1 genome, and the loss of the stop codon upstream of the yellow florescence protein (YFP) gene.
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the system and established knowledge of Cre-lox recombination

claim: YFP expression is conserved in the following progeny cells of the initial cell that taken up the plasmid.
source: Since YFP expression is genetically activated, it is conserved in the following progeny cells of the initial cell that taken up the plasmid.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of genetic inheritance

claim: This model provides, for the first time, a promising tool to study the biology of MmuPV1 infection and its target cells along with the impact of the virus on these cells.
source: This model provides, for the first time, a promising tool to study the biology of MmuPV1 infection and its target cells along with the impact of the virus on these cells.

claim: Using flow-cytometry analysis, increased proliferation dynamics were observed in MmuPV1-treated tissues.
source: Using flow-cytometry analysis, we observed increased proliferation dynamics and decreased MHC-I cell surface expression in MmuPV1-treated tissues which could have implications in tissue regenerative capacity and ability to clear the virus.

claim: Using flow-cytometry analysis, decreased MHC-I cell surface expression was observed in MmuPV1-treated tissues.
source: Using flow-cytometry analysis, we observed increased proliferation dynamics and decreased MHC-I cell surface expression in MmuPV1-treated tissues which could have implications in tissue regenerative capacity and ability to clear the virus.

claim: Increased proliferation dynamics and decreased MHC-I cell surface expression in MmuPV1-treated tissues could have implications in tissue regenerative capacity and ability to clear the virus.
source: Using flow-cytometry analysis, we observed increased proliferation dynamics and decreased MHC-I cell surface expression in MmuPV1-treated tissues which could have implications in tissue regenerative capacity and ability to clear the virus.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the implications of the observed effects

claim: A major challenge in the field has been the lack of tools to identify, observe, and characterize individually the papillomavirus hosting cells and also trace the progeny of these cells over time.
source: To date, a major challenge in the field has been the lack of tools to identify, observe, and characterize individually the papillomavirus hosting cells and also trace the progeny of these cells over time.
